name: Adam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of five on a big dairy farm, three hundred cows, with maize and grass for silage on about four hundred hectares. I'm not the manager, but I'm the one the manager rings when he's away. Mornings I'm doing the feed, mixing the ration in the feeder wagon, then it's slurry, cows to the vet, whatever's on the list. On Saturdays I run my own little contracting business, hedge-cutting and carting bales with a tractor and trailer I bought second-hand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the contracting most, honestly, because it's mine. Every hedge I cut, I get paid for, and I set the price. What wears me out is the forms, and the rules that change every year, and the bank taking a week to answer a simple question.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I plan the ration with an AI assistant, I use it for quotes and invoices for the contracting, and I ask it about anything I don't know, from a cow's symptoms to how to fix the hydraulics. I'm single, I rent a bungalow in the village, and I've got a good chunk saved, plus the tractor and trailer, which are worth a fair bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and nothing more, so people can stop panicking. I'd probably post that the farmers who used it well got a small edge, and the rest didn't miss much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I carry on with the plan: work the dairy, grow the contracting, and maybe go full-time on my own in a few years. AI saves me a few hours a week on the paperwork, and that's worth it. Nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy a second tractor next year so I can take on more contracting work, maybe hire a lad at weekends. Keep using the AI for quotes and invoices. Keep saving for a deposit on a small bit of land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. If anything, a bit pleased that the people who said it was the end of the world look silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who were you thinking of, when you said people look silly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a man at the pub who's been saying for two years that robots will take every job. He doesn't farm, he sells insurance. I'd enjoy buying him a drink and saying nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a lad at weekends rather than doing it all yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can't be in two places, and there's always a young lad who wants to learn. I learned from a contractor who let me ride along when I was fifteen. I'd want to do the same.

S0.say: I'd say it's a decent tool and nothing more, so people can stop panicking. Farmers who used it well got a small edge, and the rest didn't miss much.
S0.think: For me it means the plan carries on: work the dairy, grow my contracting business and maybe go full-time on my own. AI saves me a few hours a week, which is worth it.
S0.do: Buys a second tractor next year to take on more contracting work and hires a young lad at weekends. Keeps using AI for quotes and invoices and keeps saving for a land deposit.
S0.feel: Calm, and a bit pleased that the doom-sayers look silly.
S0.quote: He doesn't farm, he sells insurance.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is a natural small businessman who sees his Saturday contracting as his real future. He uses AI every day without fuss. His wish to take on a young apprentice came from his own experience at fifteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to work. The machines will need people to buy them, run them and fix them, and that's a business. I'd tell young farmers to get stuck in, not sit about waiting for government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good, I think. The dairy might cut a job or two, maybe mine eventually, but I'd have the contracting. If I bought a robot hedge-cutter or a mapping drone early, I'd be the one offering it to the small farms that can't buy their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at buying one robot machine for the contracting in the first year, probably something for spraying or weeding, using part of my savings. I'd learn it inside out and take it round the small farms. If it paid, I'd buy a second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Keen, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your savings would you put in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe half, which is a lot. But I'd still have the tractor, the job at the dairy and the other half. If it failed, I'd sell the robot second-hand and lose a bit, not everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on the dairy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, probably. He's in his fifties, does the milking and won't touch a phone. I'd try to talk him into helping with the contracting, because he's a brilliant driver. But I don't think he'd want to work for someone half his age.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to work, because machines need people to buy, run and fix them. I'd tell young farmers to get stuck in instead of waiting for government help.
S1.think: For me it's good, even if the dairy cuts jobs, because I'd have the contracting. If I bought a robot machine early, I'd be the one offering it to small farms that can't buy their own.
S1.do: Puts about half his savings into one robot sprayer or weeder for his contracting business in the first year. Learns it thoroughly, takes it round small farms and buys a second if it pays.
S1.quote: If it failed, I'd sell the robot second-hand and lose a bit, not everything.
S1.fieldNote: He sees disruption as a business opening and is ready to risk half his savings on it. He had a clear exit if it went wrong. His concern for an older colleague was real, though he expected pride to get in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so get moving. The people who move first will do fine and the ones who wait for the government will be waiting a long time. I'd still say that, even if it made me unpopular at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years worries me more than I'd say. If AI can do almost any work, then my contracting is up against big companies with fleets of robots and money I'll never have. I'd be fine for cash for a while, but my plan of being my own boss might get squashed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the second-hand tractor straight away while it's still worth something, and buy the best robot I could afford. I'd leave the dairy early to go full-time contracting, before they let me go. And I'd try to sign up the small farms round here on contracts before the big firms arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and uneasy at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the people who wait for government will wait a long time. Would you take any government help yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if I could help it. But if they offered cheap loans for small businesses to buy machines, I'd be first in the queue. That's not a handout, that's a loan, I'd pay it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I have one go at it, and if I pick the wrong machine I'm finished. With ten years I'd learn as I go and make mistakes slowly. The fast one rewards the person who already has the money, and that's not me, not really.

S2.say: I'd say it's here, so get moving, because people who wait for the government will wait a long time. I'd say that even if it made me unpopular at the pub.
S2.think: Two years worries me more than I'd admit, because my contracting would face big companies with robot fleets and money I'll never have. I'd be fine for cash, but my plan to be my own boss might get squashed.
S2.do: Sells his second-hand tractor at once to buy the best robot he can afford. Leaves the dairy early to go full-time contracting and signs up local small farms on contracts before big firms arrive.
S2.feel: Uneasy and excited at the same time.
S2.quote: The fast one rewards the person who already has the money, and that's not me, not really.
S2.fieldNote: His public confidence hides a private fear that big companies would crush his small business. He would move fast and sell assets to get in early. He drew a firm line between loans, which he'd take, and handouts, which he wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you're willing to work and take a risk. I'd say young people should be learning to run the machines and starting their own businesses. Less moaning, more doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years suits me, honestly. Enough time to build the contracting into a proper business before the big firms get here. Not so long that everyone else catches up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy one robot, prove it on a few farms, and buy a second by the end of year two. I'd go part-time at the dairy, then leave once the contracting paid my rent. I'd take on an apprentice, maybe Kev's grandson, who's sixteen and mad on machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the start of silage season, busy and ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not so long that everyone else catches up. Is there a part of you that wants others to be slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, a bit, yes. That's business. But I'd still help anyone who asked, I'm not going to pretend I'm the only one who deserves a go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the contracting once full AGI arrived in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't see. Maybe the robots run themselves and I'm just the man who owns them and the contracts. That's still a business. Or maybe the big firms swallow me. I'd want to be big enough by then to sell up for a good price.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty if you're willing to work and take a risk. Young people should learn to run the machines and start their own businesses, with less moaning and more doing.
S3.think: Five years suits me, because it's enough time to build the contracting into a proper business before big firms arrive. It's not so long that everyone else catches up.
S3.do: Buys one robot in the first year, proves it on a few farms and buys a second by the end of year two. Goes part-time at the dairy, then leaves once contracting pays his rent, and takes on a colleague's sixteen-year-old grandson as an apprentice.
S3.feel: Calm, busy and ready, like the start of silage season.
S3.quote: I'd want to be big enough by then to sell up for a good price.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is his ideal: time to build, but an early-mover edge. He admitted, laughing, that part of him wants others to be slow. His end game is to own the machines and contracts or sell the business at a good price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd also say the government should cut the red tape so small businesses can actually buy and run these machines. Half my time already goes on forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is good for me, but it's also good for everyone else, so it's more of a fair race. I'd be thirty-seven, with a proper business if I've done it right. I'd worry more about the young lads in the village with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the contracting steadily, one machine at a time, and keep my job at the dairy for a few more years for the steady pay. I'd write to the local councillor about the planning rules for machine sheds, which are a nightmare. And I'd take on apprentices, because if there's ten years' warning, someone should be training the next lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless about the forms, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about the young lads in the village. What about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If all the work goes, what do they do with their days? I grew up working on farms every summer, and it kept me out of trouble. Machines don't need a lad to hold the gate open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Of the three AGI pictures, which suits you best?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The five-year one for my business, the ten-year one for everyone else. With ten years I'd still do well, just with more competition. I can live with that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it, and the government should cut red tape so small businesses can buy and run these machines. Half my time already goes on forms.
S4.think: Ten years is good for me but also for everyone else, so it's a fairer race. I'd worry more about the young lads in the village with nothing to do.
S4.do: Grows his contracting business one machine at a time while keeping his dairy job for steady pay. Writes to the local councillor about planning rules for machine sheds and takes on apprentices.
S4.feel: Calm, though a bit restless about the paperwork.
S4.quote: Machines don't need a lad to hold the gate open.
S4.fieldNote: He was candid that the five-year timeline suits his business best, while ten years is fairer to everyone else. His political ask is less red tape, not more support. His concern turned to young people losing the summer work that shaped him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because only the people who already have money get to move. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses to buy machines, and the government getting out of the way on planning and forms. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about apprentices. Everyone talks about jobs going, nobody talks about who teaches the next lot. If I can train a sixteen-year-old to run a robot sprayer, that's worth more than any scheme from the ministry.

headlineQuote: Every hedge I cut, I get paid for, and I set the price.
portrait: Adam Hansen, 27, works on a large dairy farm and runs his own weekend contracting business with a second-hand tractor and trailer. He's single, uses AI every day, has strong savings and wants to be his own boss. He shrugs off the AI Plateau and sees Steady Disruption as a business chance worth half his savings. AGI by 2028 makes him uneasy, because big firms with money could squash him, but five or ten years look like a race he can win, and he worries most about young people losing the work that shaped him.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because only people who already have money would get to move in time.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small businesses to buy machines and less red tape on planning and forms, a fair start rather than handouts.
